xs: **Jet streams** and **ocean currents** are **factors (controls)** of climate.
22.x: Jet streams and ocean currents are factors (controls) of climate.

22.s: The current IMD rainfall normal for the southwest monsoon season, based on the 1971–2020 period, is:
22.x: The IMD normal rainfall for June–September, based on the 1971–2020 base period, is 868.6 mm.
xs: IMD's SW monsoon (**Jun-Sep**) normal (LPA) is **868.6 mm** — option **(2)**.
It is based on the **1971-2020** period.
xa: WMO standard climate period: **30 years**.
Elements of climate: temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, **precipitation**, cloudiness.
About **40** coastal districts may warm by over **1** degC by **2040**; **AP and Tamil Nadu** to get excess SW-monsoon rain.
22.tq: Separate the precise normal value from nearby numerical distractors.

22.s: Which one of the following is NOT regarded as a control of climate?
22.x: Distance from a river is not a recognised control of climate. Latitude, altitude and distance from the sea influence climatic conditions.
xs: **Distance from a river** is **not** a control of climate — option **(3)** (APPSC GS **2025**).
**Latitude** (angle of rays, insolation), **altitude** (lapse rate) and **distance from the sea** (equable vs continental) are true controls.
xa: Other controls: **mountain barriers/relief**, **ocean currents**, **winds and pressure belts**.
**Himalayas** keep north India **3-8 deg C** warmer in winter.

o: The Earth's rotation on its axis
Convergence of the two equatorial currents

26.s: Which one among the following is not a cause of generation of ocean currents?

26.s:
Consider the following statements.

II. The planetary winds are probably the dominant influence on the flow of ocean currents.
III. The water of high salinity are denser than the water of low salinity.
IV. A landmass always obstructs and diverts an ocean current.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
26.x: Currents are surface water circulating in regular patterns (I), driven mainly by planetary winds (II), and saltier water is denser (III). A landmass deflects but does not always obstruct a current, so IV is false.

26.s:

26.x: Currents are slow surface movements (1), help keep the heat balance (2), are set in motion mainly by prevailing winds (3) and are affected by the ocean's configuration (4): all four.

26.s: Ocean waves mainly carry what?

26.s: Which one of the following best describes a tide?
o: An irregular rise of sea level caused by storm winds
A permanent increase in sea level caused by melting ice
A circular movement of ocean water caused by the Coriolis force
A periodic rise and fall of sea level occurring once or twice a day
26.x: A tide is the periodic rise and fall of sea level, generally occurring once or twice a day. Storm surges are irregular and weather-driven phenomena.
xs: A **tide** is the **periodic rise and fall of sea level once or twice a day** — option **(4)**.
It is caused by the **gravitational pull of the moon** (greater) and **sun** (lesser), countered by **centrifugal force**.
An irregular rise from storm winds is a **storm surge** — weather-driven, irregular, **unlike tides**.
xa: High tides recur about every **12 h 25 min**.
**Semi-diurnal** (two highs + two lows a day) is the **most common** type.
Tidal energy: **tidal range** (barrage across an estuary) vs **tidal stream** (underwater turbines).
26.tq: Use the precise definition and distinguish tides from storm surges.

26.s: Which component of tide-generating force is more important?
xs: The **horizontal components** of tide-generating force matter **more than the vertical**.
26.x: The horizontal components of tide-generating force matter more than the vertical.

26.s: Storm surges are caused by what?
o: Pull of the Moon and Sun
xs: **storm surges** are caused by **winds + pressure changes** — weather-driven and **irregular**, unlike tides.
26.x: storm surges are caused by winds + pressure changes — weather-driven and irregular, unlike tides.

26.s: Tidal energy can be harnessed through
o: only wind turbines placed on beaches
barrages across estuaries and underwater turbines
desalination plants located on continental shelves
26.x: Tidal energy is harnessed through tidal-range systems, such as barrages across estuaries, and tidal-stream systems using underwater turbines.
xs: Tidal energy is harnessed by **barrages across estuaries** and **underwater turbines** — option **(3)**.
**Tidal range** systems use a **barrage across an estuary**; **tidal stream** systems use **underwater turbines**.
Beach wind turbines, inland river dams and desalination plants are not tidal-energy technologies.
xa: **Gulf of Khambhat** has a potential of ~**7,000 MW**, among the world's most significant.
**Bay of Fundy** (Canada) has the **world's greatest tidal range**.
Tidal water channelled into **bays/estuaries** forms **tidal currents**.
26.tq: Distinguish the two technological methods from unrelated coastal infrastructure.

26.s: Which factor drives deep thermohaline circulation?

26.x: density differences do matter — saltier, colder water sinks, driving deep thermohaline circulation.

26.s: What is the main driver of ordinary ocean waves?
xs: Waves are **oscillatory movements** of water that **mainly transfer energy**; **wind** is the **main driver**.
xa: **Tsunamis** have **different causes** from wind-driven waves; wave **timing** is **variable**.

26.s: Waves are what kind of movement of water?
xs: Waves are **oscillatory movements** of water that **mainly transfer energy**; **wind** is the **main driver**.

26.s: Tides are what kind of changes in water level?
xs: Nature: **Oscillatory movements** of **water** — mainly **transfer energy**; **Vertical** and **periodic changes** in **water level** — **periodic changes** in **sea level**; **Continuous directed movements** of water — **horizontal movement** of **water**
26.x: Nature: Oscillatory movements of water — mainly transfer energy; Vertical and periodic changes in water level — periodic changes in sea level; Continuous directed movements of water — horizontal movement of water

26.s: Which of the following is associated with tides?
26.x: Tides are linked with tidal energy. Continuous flow describes currents and oscillation describes waves.
xs: **Tidal energy** is associated with tides — option **(1)** is correct.
Tides' key effects: **tidal energy** and **spring/neap** patterns.
**Continuous directed movement** = **currents**; **oscillatory movement** and **variable timing** = **waves**.
xa: Tidal energy: **tidal range** (barrage) vs **tidal stream** (underwater turbines).
**Gulf of Khambhat**: range **5-10 m**, potential ~**7,000 MW**.
**Gulf of Kutch** **5-8 m**; **Sundarbans** ~**5 m**.
26.tq: Discriminate currents, tides and waves.

26.s: Which factor blocks and redirects currents along landmasses?
xs: **Coastline configuration** **deflects or redirects** currents; **ocean-floor relief** **modifies current direction**.
26.x: Coastline configuration deflects or redirects currents; ocean-floor relief modifies current direction.

26.s: Wave height is measured from where to where?
xs: **wave height** = **crest to trough**; time between crests is the **period**.
26.x: wave height = crest to trough; time between crests is the period.

26.s: The distance from one crest to the next is called?
xs: **Breakers** form when depth < **half the wavelength**.
xa: **wavelength** = **crest to crest**.
26.x: Breakers form when depth < half the wavelength.

26.s: Slow, steady, long-period waves from distant storms are called?
xs: **Swells** are **slow, steady, long-period waves** that come from **distant storms**
xa: **Kallakkadal** (Kerala swell surge): long-period swells (**30-300 s**) from southern Indian Ocean storms ~**10,000 km** away.
Short, steep waves from **local winds** are young wind waves, not swells.

26.s: Narrow, fast channels of water flowing away from the shore are called?
xs: Narrow channels flowing **away from shore** are **rip currents**; sea-floor displacement produces a **tsunami**.
26.x: Narrow channels flowing away from shore are rip currents; sea-floor displacement produces a tsunami.

26.s: A wave approaching a shore generally breaks when:
o: Its crest becomes equal to its trough
The wind ceases in the open ocean
The water depth becomes less than half the wavelength
The water depth becomes greater than the wavelength
26.x: Near the shore, friction slows the wave. It breaks when the water depth is less than half its wavelength.
xs: A wave breaks when the **water depth becomes less than half the wavelength** — option **(3)**.
Near the shore, waves **slow by friction** with the sea floor; these are **breakers**.
Crest and trough are the **top** and **bottom** of a wave; they never become "equal", so option (1) is meaningless.
xa: **Wavelength** = crest to crest; wave **height** = crest to trough; **period** = time between crests.
**Rip currents**: narrow, fast channels flowing **away from shore** as shoreward water escapes through a narrow path.
**ISRO** project: **AI + satellite** tools to detect **rip currents** for beach safety.
26.tq: Recall the threshold ratio used to identify the formation of breakers.

26.s: Kallakkadal, observed along the Kerala coast, is associated with:
o: A tidal bore caused by the full Moon
Long-period swell surges from storms in the southern Indian Ocean
Short wind waves generated within the Arabian Sea
A sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor near Kerala
26.x: Kallakkadal is a swell surge produced by long-period swells generated by storms in the southern Indian Ocean.
xs: **Kallakkadal** is caused by **long-period swell surges** from **storms in the southern Indian Ocean** — option **(2)**.
These swells (**30-300 s**) travel ~**10,000 km** to reach the **Kerala** coast; most frequent **pre-monsoon**.
It is not local wind waves (those are short and steep) nor a sea-floor displacement (that is a **tsunami**).
xa: **Swells** = slow, steady, **long-period** waves from **distant storms**.
**INCOIS** (Hyderabad) issues **swell-surge** alerts and has a **Coastal Flood Monitoring System** at **Kollam** harbour.
⚠ A **storm surge** is different: a weather-driven rise from **winds + pressure changes**.
26.tq: Link the regional term with its specific wave phenomenon and source.

26.s: Tsunamis are caused by sudden vertical displacement of what?

26.x: A tsunami comes from sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor (quake, landslide, volcano).

26.s: What kind of wavelength do tsunamis have?

26.s: Which one of the following correctly describes a rip current?
o: A tidal current flowing only towards the beach
A broad current flowing parallel to the coastline
A deep-ocean current caused exclusively by salinity differences
A narrow, fast channel flowing away from the shore
26.x: A rip current is a narrow and fast-moving channel of water flowing away from the shore.
xs: A **rip current** is a **narrow, fast channel flowing away from the shore** — option **(4)**.

Density/salinity-driven flow is the deep **thermohaline** circulation, not a rip current.

26.s: Which tide has the minimum tidal range?
xs: **Spring tide** = **maximum** tidal range; **neap tide** = **minimum**.

26.s: Spring tides occur at which Moon phases?
xs: Spring: **new moon or full moon**, effects **reinforce**; neap: **first or third quarter**, effects **partially opposing**.
26.x: Spring: new moon or full moon, effects reinforce; neap: first or third quarter, effects partially opposing.

26.s: Which body's gravitational pull is greater in producing tides?
xs: The **moon's** pull is **greater**, the **sun's** lesser.

26.s: The tidal bulge on the side opposite the Moon is associated with which force?
xs: The bulge on the **opposite side** comes from **centrifugal force** (the **indirect tide**).

26.s: The tidal bulge facing the Moon is called what?
xs: The bulge **facing the moon** is the **direct tide** (gravitational attraction).

26.x: The bulge facing the moon is the direct tide (gravitational attraction).

26.s: Tides of unequal height are called what?
xs: **Mixed** = tides of **unequal height**; **Spring** = **highest range** (highest high, lowest low).
26.x: Mixed = tides of unequal height; Spring = highest range (highest high, lowest low).

26.s: Which tide has the highest tidal range?
xs: Spring tide: sun, moon and earth **in a line** — at **new moon and full moon**.
xa: **Neap tide**: sun and moon at **right angles**, ~**7 days** after spring — **lowest range**.
26.x: Spring tide: sun, moon and earth in a line — at new moon and full moon.

26.s: The interval between successive high tides is approximately

Most coasts get **semi-diurnal** tides: **two high + two low** tides a day.
**7 days** is the gap between a **spring** and the following **neap** tide, not between high tides.
xa: **Diurnal** tide = one high + one low a day; **mixed** = unequal heights.
⚠ **Spring** = sun, moon, earth in a line (new/full moon); **Neap** = right angles (first/third quarter).
**Perigean tides**: moon **closest** → unusually high.

26.s: Perigean tides are unusually high because the Moon is
o: at right angles to the Sun

xs: **Perigean tides** are unusually high because the moon is **closest to the earth** — option **(4)**.
The **moon's** gravitational pull has the **greater** effect on tides, so a nearer moon raises them more.
Sun and moon at **right angles** give **neap tides** — the **lowest** range, not high tides.
xa: **Spring tides**: sun, moon and earth **in a line** — **new moon and full moon** — highest range.
**Tide-generating force** = gravitational attraction − centrifugal force.
Bulge facing the moon = **direct tide**; opposite = **indirect tide** (centrifugal).

26.s: ITEWS is a UNESCO regional tsunami service provider for how many Indian Ocean countries?

26.s: The Equatorial Counter Current is best described as a current that flows:
o: From south to north only in the Indian Ocean
From north to south along the western coasts of continents
From east to west between the polar currents
From west to east between the North and South Equatorial Currents

xs: The **Equatorial Counter Current** flows **west to east** between the **North and South Equatorial Currents** — option **(4)**.

26.s: Large circular ocean current systems are called what?
xs: **gyres** are large **circular current systems** formed by **winds, Coriolis force and land barriers**.

26.s: In which direction do gyres circulate in the Northern Hemisphere?
xs: **clockwise in the NH**, **anticlockwise in the SH**.

26.s: Which one of the following forms the northern boundary of the Sargasso Sea?

xa: The Sargasso Sea is the only sea bounded by **currents, not land** — "sea without shores".

26.s: The Sargasso Sea is unusual because it is
o: the only sea bounded by ocean currents rather than land
a sea enclosed entirely by coral reefs
the only sea located in the Southern Hemisphere

26.s: The mild climate of north-western Europe and the ice-free condition of ports such as those in Norway and Murmansk are associated with the

26.s: Which one of the following ocean currents is correctly classified as a cold current of the Indian Ocean?

26.s: Which one of the following is the correct classification of the Agulhas, Brazil and Humboldt currents respectively?

47.s: Which of the following correctly defines wasteland?

xs: **Wasteland** is **degraded land that can be brought under vegetative cover with reasonable effort**, so option **(1)** is correct.
It is not land left fallow for one season (that is **current fallow**), nor permanently barren land.
xa: It is mapped under **National Wastelands Monitoring** using **IRS** data (IRS commissioned **1988**).
**Culturable wasteland** = uncultivated for **more than 5 years**.
**Barren and unculturable land** is a separate land-use class.
47.tq: Reject the extreme definition that treats all degraded land as permanently unusable.

The global response was the **UNCCD** (**1994**).

37.s: Which of the following rivers originates from Mahabaleshwar in the Western Ghats?

37.s: Which of the following rivers of India does not originate from the Western Ghats?
37.x: The Tapi rises at Multai in Betul district of MP on the Satpura plateau, not in the Western Ghats. The Godavari, Cauvery and Kabini (Kabam) rise in the Western Ghats.

37.s: Which of the following rivers rises from the Trimbak Hills in Nasik district?
37.x: The Vaitarna rises in the Trimbak hills of Nashik district and flows west to the Arabian Sea north of Mumbai. The Shetrunji and Dhadhar are Gujarat rivers; the Bhadra rises in the Western Ghats of Karnataka.

37.s: The source of Cauvery River lies in –
37.x: The Cauvery rises at Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri hills of Kodagu, Karnataka. Gavilgarh hills are in Vidarbha and Amarkantak is the source of the Narmada and Son.

37.s: Sone, Narmada, and Mahanadi originate from
37.x: The Narmada and Son rise on the Amarkantak plateau (Maikal range); the small Mahanadi that joins the Son also rises there, while the main Mahanadi rises nearby at Sihawa. The Eastern Ghats, Aravallis and Palamu hills are wrong.

37.s: Which one of the following is the actual source of the Sone river?
37.x:
Printed key and most general books: Amarkantak (Sonmuda). The 'actual' source asked here: Son Bachharwar near Pendra, then in Bilaspur district.
The Son is usually said to rise at Amarkantak (Sonmuda), but its actual source lies near Pendra, at Sonbachharwar village in Pendra tehsil, then in Bilaspur district (now Gaurela-Pendra-Marwahi, Chhattisgarh) – the answer the word 'actual' points to.

37.s: Which of the following three rivers of the Peninsular India have the Amarkantak region as their source?
37.x: The Son and Narmada rise at Amarkantak, and the Mahanadi rises in the same Maikal–Chhattisgarh upland (Sihawa; a small Mahanadi stream also joins the Son there). Krishna, Godavari and Kaveri rise in the Western Ghats; Chambal, Betwa and Luni elsewhere.

37.s: Narmada river originates
37.x: The Narmada rises at Amarkantak in the Maikal range (Anuppur, MP). Bhedaghat (Jabalpur), Shahdol and Hoshangabad are places on or near its course.

37.s: Son, Narmada, and Mahanadi originate from –
37.x: The Son and Narmada rise at Amarkantak; the Mahanadi rises nearby at Sihawa in the same upland. They do not rise in the Palamu hills, Eastern Ghats or Aravallis.

37.s: Which of the following rivers does NOT have its origin in the Amarkantak Plateau?
37.x: The Damodar rises at Khamarpat hill on the Chota Nagpur plateau, not at Amarkantak. The Narmada, Son and Johilla (a Son tributary) rise on the Amarkantak plateau.

37.s: Which one of the following rivers originates at Amarkantak?
37.x: The Narmada originates at Amarkantak and flows west in a rift valley. The Damodar rises in Chota Nagpur, the Mahanadi at Sihawa and the Tapi at Multai.

37.s: At which one of the following places do two important rivers of India originate, while one flows northward to merge with another major river flowing towards the Bay of Bengal and the other flows towards the Arabian Sea?
37.x: At Amarkantak both the Son (flows north and joins the Ganga, which reaches the Bay of Bengal) and the Narmada (flows west to the Arabian Sea) originate.

37.s: At which one of the following places do two important rivers of India originate while one of them flows towards north and merges with another important river flowing towards the Bay of Bengal, the other one flows towards the Arabian Sea?
37.x: Amarkantak: the Son flows north to merge with the Ganga (Bay of Bengal), and the Narmada flows west to the Arabian Sea.

37.s:
Why is the Godavari River also known as the Dakshin Ganga?
1. It flows through vast plains, covering about 1500 km.
2. It has a similar drainage pattern with numerous tributaries joining them along their course.
3. It originates in the Himalayas.

37.src: AP recruitment paper (header page missing in scan)

Peninsular rivers are rain-fed and non-perennial; in Maharashtra the Godavari dries to a trickle in summer, the Kaveri does not flow there and the Narmada only skirts the MP–Maharashtra border, so the key is 'None of these'.

37.s: Into how many branches does the Godavari river split before joining Bay of Bengal?

37.src: Assistant Director of Fisheries in AP Fisheries Service 2017

Rocket AP Geography: 7 branches (the 'Sapta Godavari' mouths). Strictly the Godavari first splits at Dowleswaram into 2 main branches, the Gautami and the Vasishta, which then divide further; the printed key 4 has no source.
The Godavari splits into the Gautami and Vasishta and then into seven branches (Sapta Godavari) before entering the Bay of Bengal; 4 has no support.

37.s: Which of the following is the correct order of rivers from North to South?
37.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer (Mains) Paper-I General Studies

Indus (Ladakh) – Ganga (northern plains) – Godavari – Krishna runs strictly from north to south, the key. Ganga – Mahanadi – Godavari – Krishna is also north-to-south, so the stem is loose; Yamuna–Ganga and Narmada–Kaveri orders are not clean.

37.s:
Which of the following statements is/are correct about the rivers of India?
A. The main Himalayan river systems are the Ganga, the Indus and the Brahmaputra river systems.
B. The main peninsular river systems include the Narmada, the Tapi, the Godavari, the Krishna, the Kaveri and the Mahanadi river systems.
C. The Indus originates in the northern slopes of the Kailash range in Tibet near Lake Manasarovar.
37.x: All three are true: the Himalayan systems are the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; the main Peninsular systems are the Narmada, Tapi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Mahanadi; and the Indus rises on the northern slopes of the Kailash range near Lake Mansarovar (Bokhar Chu glacier).

37.s: Which of the following rivers divides the Deccan Tableland from Northern India?
37.x: The Narmada flows in a rift valley between the Vindhyas (north) and Satpuras (south), so it separates the Deccan Tableland from northern India. Krishna and Godavari lie wholly within the Peninsula; the Chambal drains the Malwa to the Yamuna.

37.s: Which one of the following east-flowing rivers of India has a rift valley due to down-warping?

37.s: Which of the following rivers is an example of the superimposed river?

37.s: Which of the following rivers flows through a rift valley?
37.x:
Most books and keys: Narmada. The Damodar also flows in a rift valley (Gondwana trough), so option 1 is defensible.
The Narmada is the classic rift-valley river, flowing in a fault trough between the Vindhyas and Satpuras. The Damodar's Gondwana trough is also called a rift valley, but the question's intended answer is the Narmada; the Kosi and Godavari are not rift-valley rivers in the textbooks.

37.x: The Narmada flows through the Marble Rocks gorge at Bhedaghat near Jabalpur, where it forms the Dhuandhar falls.

33.s: One of the main characteristics of retreating Monsoon is?
o: Strengthen low pressure region over North west India
Cause for rise in temperatures throughout India
Cause for shifting of low pressure area to North
Origin of Cyclonic Storms in Bay of Bengal
33.src: Assistant Social BC, Tribal Welfare Officers Mains Paper-I 2
33.x: The retreating monsoon season is known for tropical cyclones that originate mainly in the Bay of Bengal. The low over NW India weakens and shifts south, and temperatures fall, so the other options are wrong.

33.s: Retreating monsoon blows towards?
o: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal
33.x: The retreating (north-east) monsoon winds blow from the land south-eastward towards the Bay of Bengal, pick up moisture there and rain on the Coromandel coast.

33.s:
Consider the following statements:
1.
Assertion (A): Anti-cyclonic conditions are formed in the winter season when atmospheric pressure is high, and air temperatures are low.
2.
Reason (R): Winter rainfall in Northern India causes the development of anticyclonic conditions with low temperatures. Options:
o: Both A and R are individually true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are individually true, but R is NOT a correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
33.x: A is true: winter anticyclonic conditions develop because the cold land makes the air dense, giving high pressure and low temperature. R is false: winter rain from western disturbances does not create the anticyclone.

33.s:
Assertion (A) : Anti-cyclonic conditions are formed in winter season when atmospheric pressure is high and air temperature is low.
Reason (R) : Winter rainfall in Northern India causes development of anticyclonic conditions with low temperature.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct
33.x: A is true: winter anticyclonic conditions develop because the cold land makes the air dense, giving high pressure and low temperature. R is false: winter rain from western disturbances does not create the anticyclone.

33.s: Which one of the following is not associated with monsoon climate in India?
o: South-Equatorial warm currents of Indian Ocean
33.x: Western disturbances are Mediterranean temperate cyclones of the winter season and are not part of the monsoon system; El Nino, Indian Ocean currents and Bay of Bengal cyclones are linked with the monsoon.

33.s: The frequency of cyclones is highest during the following months.
33.x: Tropical cyclones are most frequent in the retreating-monsoon months of October–November, mainly in the Bay of Bengal.

33.s: Which one of the following is not correct regarding South India?
o: Diurnal range of temperature is less.
Annual range of temperature is less.
Temperature is high throughout the year.
33.x: South India has a maritime climate with small diurnal and annual ranges and high temperatures all year, so extreme climatic conditions are not found there; extremes belong to the continental north.

33.s:
Given below are two statements, in which one if labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : During the winter season, most part of India is dry.
Reason (R) : Most parts of the country are under influence of the northeast trade winds during the winter season.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is the correct
33.x: Both are true and R explains A: in winter most of India is under the north-east trade winds, which blow from land to sea and carry little moisture, so the season is dry (only ~2% of annual rain). The option wording is garbled; option 4 is 'both true, R is the correct explanation'.

33.s: Where can one expect dry winter in India ?
33.x: The Bengal (lower Ganga) plains have the Koeppen Cwg type – monsoon with dry winter. J&K and the Punjab–Haryana plains get western-disturbance rain or snow in winter, and Tamil Nadu gets its main rain from the NE monsoon in winter.

33.s: Of the following, the state which receives rainfall in winter season is
33.x: Tamil Nadu gets its main rain in winter from the north-east monsoon (October–December); Kerala, West Bengal and Odisha are mainly SW-monsoon fed.

33.s: Which one of the following places has the lowest rainfall during the South-West Monsoon?
33.x: Chennai lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats and the Bay branch blows parallel to the Tamil Nadu coast, so it gets the least SW-monsoon rain; its main rain comes from the NE monsoon.

33.s: How do the 'western disturbances' affect the crops in North India?
o: They cause heavy damage to the standing crops
They bring in locusts which destroy the crops
They are beneficial to the crops by causing winter rain
They help in keeping the plants warm to some extent in winter
33.x: Western disturbances bring 10–15 cm of winter rain to north-west India, which is very beneficial to the rabi (wheat) crop; they do not bring locusts or mainly damage crops.

33.s: The retreating monsoon in India causes?
33.x: During the retreat of the monsoon, clear skies and high humidity make the weather hot and oppressive – the 'October heat'.

33.s:
What would be the influence on the weather conditions when in mid-winter a feeble high pressure develops over the North-Western part of India?
I. High and dry winds would blow outward from this high pressure area.
II. The Northern plain would become cold.
III. Scorching winds (locally called loo) would blow during the day time.
IV. There would be torrential rains brought up by thunderstorms.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
33.x: A feeble winter high over NW India sends dry winds outward and the northern plains turn cold, so I and II are correct. Loo and thunderstorm rains belong to the hot season, not mid-winter.

33.s: South Arcot and Ramanathapuram receive over 50 per cent of their annual rainfall from which one of the following?
o: Bay of Bengal branch of summer monsoon.
33.x: South Arcot and Ramanathapuram are on the Tamil Nadu (Coromandel) coast, which is dry in the SW monsoon and gets over half its rain from the north-east monsoon.

33.s: Which one of the following causes rainfall in the North-Western parts of India during winter season?
33.x: Winter rain in north-west India comes from western disturbances – temperate cyclones from the Mediterranean.

33.s:
Declining of monsoon is indicated by
I. clear sky.
II. pressure condition in Bay of Bengal.
III. rising temperature on land.
Select your answer using the following Codes
33.x: Monsoon withdrawal is marked by clear skies, the change in pressure as the low shifts to the Bay of Bengal, and rising land temperatures ('October heat') – all three.

33.s: Which of the following areas of India receives winter rainfall ?
33.x: Western disturbances bring winter rain to the north-west (Punjab, Haryana, J&K, Himachal). The south-west of India is dry in winter. The south-east (Tamil Nadu) also gets NE-monsoon rain, but the classic answer to 'winter rainfall' is the north-west.

33.s: Winter rainfall in Tamil Nadu is mostly due to –
33.x: Tamil Nadu's winter rain comes from the north-east monsoon (October–December), not from western disturbances.

33.s: Which are the months for monsoon usually in Tamil Nadu?
33.x: Tamil Nadu's monsoon (main rainy season) is the north-east monsoon of October–December, i.e. November–December among the options.

33.s:
Assertion (A) : Northern plains of India receive some rainfall in winter.
Reason (R) : North East Monsoon is active in winter.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is not the correct
33.x: A is true: the northern plains get some winter rain, but from western disturbances. R is true too – the NE monsoon is active in winter – but it rains on the Coromandel coast, so R does not explain A.

33.s: India's Northern plains get winter rainfall due to –
33.x: The northern plains' winter rain comes from western disturbances (Mediterranean temperate cyclones).

33.s: During the period of the south-west Monsoon, Tamil Nadu remains dry because
o: The winds do not reach this area
There are no mountains in this area
It lies in the rain-shadow area
The temperature is too high to let the winds come down
33.x: Tamil Nadu lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats for the Arabian Sea branch (and the Bay branch blows parallel to its coast), so it stays dry in the SW monsoon.

33.s: Which one of the following sets of states does not receive most of its rainfall from South-West Monsoon during the months of June to September?
o: Tamil Nadu and Jammu and Kashmir
33.x: Tamil Nadu gets most of its rain from the NE monsoon (Oct–Dec) and J&K a large share from winter western disturbances, so neither relies mainly on June–September rain.

33.s: Which one of the following places of India experiences highest atmospheric pressure during winter?
33.x:
Answer keys disagree: GKToday gives Leh, ExamRobot gives Jaisalmer (web search results); NCERT's January isobars support Jaisalmer.
In winter a high develops over north-west India – NCERT puts the 1019 mb isobar through north-west India and 1013 mb in the far south – so Jaisalmer (NW Rajasthan) has the highest pressure. Leh, at ~3,500 m, has low station pressure; Chennai and Guwahati are lower.

33.s: The winter rains caused by Western Disturbances in North-Western Plain of India gradually decreases order of their normal annual rainfall?
33.x: Western disturbances enter from the west, so their winter rain decreases from west to east across the north-western plains.

33.s: The state which receives maximum rainfall due to North-East monsoon is :
33.x: Tamil Nadu gets the largest share of its rain from the NE monsoon (Oct–Dec); Assam, West Bengal and Odisha are SW-monsoon fed.

33.s: Which of the following coastal region in India, receives rainfall from North Eastern monsoon ?
33.x: The Coromandel coast gets its main rain from the north-east monsoon; the Malabar, Konkan and Gujarat coasts get SW-monsoon rain.

33.s:
Which areas of India receive rainfall from North- East Monsoon?
A. Tamil Nadu Coast
B. Gujarat Coast
C. Southern Andhra Pradesh
D. South-East Karnataka
33.x: The NE monsoon rains on the Tamil Nadu coast, southern (coastal) Andhra Pradesh and south-east Karnataka – not the Gujarat coast.

33.s: The main reason for monsoon in India?
o: Temperature differential between the Land and Indian Ocean
Temperature differential between North and South India
Temperature differential between summer and winter
33.x: The monsoon is caused mainly by the differential heating of the land and the Indian Ocean (Halley's thermal concept): the hot land forms a low that draws moist sea winds. North–south or summer–winter contrasts and nearness to the equator are not the cause.

33.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The monsoons are primary winds.
II. The monsoons are confined only to the tropical lands lying between 20°N and 20°S.
III. Distribution of rainfall received from the South-West monsoons is governed mainly by the relief of the country.
Which of the above statements are correct?
33.src: APPSC Group-II Screening Test (General Studies & Mental Abil
33.x: Monsoons are seasonal (secondary) winds, not primary (planetary) winds, so I is false. Textbooks place the monsoon lands in the tropics between about 20°N and 20°S, and the SW-monsoon rain is governed mainly by relief, so II and III are correct.

33.s: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the monsoon in India?
o: Monsoons are known for their uncertainties
33.src: APPSC 2022 Various Non Gazetted Posts Limited Recruitment
33.x: Monsoon rain is unsteady, unevenly distributed, interrupted by breaks and uncertain, so 'equally distributed' is not a characteristic; the other three are genuine features.

33.s: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the monsoon in India?
o: Monsoons are known for their uncertainties
33.src: APPSC 2022 Various Non Gazetted Posts Limited Recruitment
33.x: Monsoon rain is unsteady, unevenly distributed, interrupted by breaks and uncertain, so 'equally distributed' is not a characteristic; the other three are genuine features.

33.s: India has an abundant volume of rainfall but is still regarded as a thirsty land. This is due to :
o: Concentration of rainfall during a few months only
33.x: India's rain comes mostly in June–September, runs off rapidly and evaporates quickly, leaving the other eight months short of water – so all three causes apply.

33.s: Amritsar and Shimla are almost on the same latitude, but their climate difference is due to-
33.x: Amritsar and Shimla lie on almost the same latitude, but Shimla (~2,200 m) is much cooler than Amritsar (~230 m) because of the difference in altitude.

33.s: Climate of India is influenced by
33.x: India's climate is controlled by its latitude (distance from the equator), relief/physiography and the Himalayas, among other factors, so all of these apply.

33.s: Climate of India is usually referred as
33.x: India's climate is the tropical monsoon type, dominated by the seasonal reversal of winds.

33.s:
Assertion (A) The monsoon winds of Southern and Eastern Asia are driven by the size of Asian landmass.
Reason (R) The wind and pressure patterns in upper air circulation are associated with generation of monsoon winds.
Codes
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A are R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
33.x: Both are true: the size of the Asian landmass creates the land–sea heating contrast, and upper-air circulation (jets, Tibetan anticyclone) is also linked with the monsoon. But R does not explain how the landmass drives the monsoon.

33.s:
Assertion(A) : India is a Monsoonal Country.
Reason (R) : The high Himalayas impart it climatic distinctiveness.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct
33.x: India's climate is essentially monsoonal, and the lofty Himalayas act as a climatic divide that traps the monsoon and blocks cold Central Asian air, giving India its distinct monsoon climate – R explains A.

33.s:
Assertion (A) : India has a tropical Monsoon type climate.
Reason (R) : India is located exactly between the tropical latitudes.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the Correct
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct
33.x: A is true: India has a tropical monsoon climate. R is false: India extends from about 8°4'N to 37°6'N, so much of it lies north of the Tropic of Cancer, not wholly within the tropics.

33.s:
Which of the following are the major factors responsible for the monsoon type of climate in India ?
I. Location
II. Thermal contrast
III. Upper air circulation
IV. The Himalayan Mountains
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
33.x: Location (latitude), the land–sea thermal contrast, upper-air circulation (jet streams) and the Himalayas are all major factors behind India's monsoon climate.

33.s: India maintained its early cultural contacts and trade links with Southeast Asia across the Bay of Bengal. For this pre-eminence of early maritime history of Bay of Bengal, which of the following could be the most convincing explanation/explanations?
o: As compared to other countries, India had better ship-building technology in ancient and medieval times.
The rulers of southern India always patronised traders, Brahmin priests and Buddhist monks in this
Monsoon winds across the Bay of Bengal facilitated sea voyages.
Both (a) and (b) are convincing explanations in this context.
33.x: The predictable monsoon winds across the Bay of Bengal let sailors go east with the summer monsoon and return with the winter monsoon – the most convincing explanation of India's early maritime contact with South-East Asia.

33.s:
Assertion (A) : Majority of the monsoon winds enter India through Palghat Pass
Reason (R): Palghat Pass is nearer to the Indian Ocean
o: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
33.x: The SW monsoon reaches India along the whole west coast and over the Bay of Bengal; the Palghat Gap only lets part of the Arabian Sea branch through into Tamil Nadu, so A ('majority') is wrong. The gap does lie close to the sea in the far south, so R is acceptable.

33.s: "Break" monsoon period occurs when
o: Monsoon winds are interrupted by hot winds from desert
High pressure regions develop in the Pacific Ocean
Monsoon trough shifts closer to the foothills of the Himalayas
33.x: A break in the monsoon occurs when the monsoon trough (ITCZ) shifts north to the Himalayan foothills: the plains get little rain while the hills get heavy rain. Hot desert winds or Pacific highs are not the mechanism.

33.s: The period of the South West monsoon in India is as
33.x: IMD's south-west monsoon season is June to September; it gives about 75% of annual rain.

33.s:
Arrange the following states on the basis of ascending dates of the onset of monsoon. I. Uttar Pradesh
II. West Bengal III. Kerala
IV. Rajasthan
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
33.x: The monsoon sets in over Kerala first (1 June), reaches West Bengal through the Bay branch, then Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan last – III, II, I, IV.

33.s:
Which of the following statements regarding South-West monsoon in India is/are correct?
I. Monsoon reaches the Malabar coast first.
II. Rajasthan does not get rainfall from South West monsoon.
III. South-West monsoon retreats when the permanent wind belts starts shifting to the South.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
33.x: I is true: the monsoon strikes the Malabar coast first. III is true: it retreats as the pressure and wind belts shift south. II is false: Rajasthan does get some SW-monsoon rain, though little.

33.s: In which of the following States does the Monsoon arrive first?
33.x: The SW monsoon reaches Kerala first, around 1 June.

33.s:
Consider the following statements and select the correct option.
Statement I: Kerala is the first Indian state to receive the southwest monsoon in early June.
Statement II: The Bay of Bengal branch causes heavy rainfall in Meghalaya.
o: None of the statements is correct
33.src: APPSC Forest Range Officer Screening Test General Studies &
33.x: Both are correct: Kerala is the first state to receive the SW monsoon in early June, and the Bay of Bengal branch gives very heavy orographic rain in Meghalaya.

33.s: Which of the following regions is not affected much by the Arabian Sea branch of Monsoon?
33.x: The Arabian Sea branch soaks the Western Ghats, the Deccan and Madhya Pradesh (via the Narmada–Tapi valleys); the Chhattisgarh Basin gets its rain mainly from the Bay of Bengal branch.

33.s: By which monsoon does Jharkhand receive rainfall?
33.x: Jharkhand gets most of its rain from the south-west monsoon (Bay of Bengal branch), June–September.

33.s: The Western Coasts of India receive very high rainfall in summer mainly due to
33.x: The high Western Ghats lie across the path of the SW monsoon and force the winds to rise, giving heavy orographic rain on the windward west coast.

33.s:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
I. Mumbai receives more rainfall than Pune because it is located at the windward side of the Western Ghats.
II. Vidarbha region experiences semi-arid climate as it is located in a rain shadow region.
III. In India, monsoon reaches Kashmir valley at the last.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
33.x: I is true: Mumbai is windward, Pune leeward. II is accepted: interior Vidarbha lies in the rain-shadow interior and is semi-arid. III is false: the monsoon reaches west Rajasthan last, not the Kashmir valley.

33.s: Monsoon season extends from?
33.x: The SW monsoon season is June–September; in the north it is effectively mid-June to mid-September.

33.s: In North India, heat waves normally occur in the following period?
33.x: IMD's heat-wave season over north India runs from March to June (peak May–June); the shorter spans leave out part of it.

33.s:
Arrange the following seasons in Chronological order according to Hindu Calendar :
(i) Autumn
(ii) Summer
(iii) Spring
(iv) Rainy Select the correct answer using the code given below:
33.x: The six seasons run Vasanta (spring, Mar–Apr), Grishma (summer, May–Jun), Varsha (rainy, Jul–Aug), Sharad (autumn, Sep–Oct), so the order is (iii), (ii), (iv), (i).

33.s: Hot weather season thunderstorms associated with violent winds and torrential down pours in West Bengal are also called as
33.src: APPSC Zilla Sainik Welfare Officer in Sainik Welfare Service
33.x: The violent pre-monsoon evening thunderstorms of West Bengal are Kaal Baisakhi (Nor'westers). Mango showers are in Kerala–Karnataka, and Loo is a hot dry wind.

33.s: Which of the following is a local storm of Bengal and Assam, useful for tea and rice cultivation ?
33.x: Norwesters (Kaal Baisakhi) are the local storms of Bengal and Assam that help tea, jute and rice. Mango and blossom showers are South Indian; Karaburan is a Central Asian wind.

33.s: Mango showers are common phenomena in which States of India?
33.x: Mango showers are the pre-monsoon showers of Kerala and coastal Karnataka that help mangoes ripen.

33.s: Rains caused by thunderstorms during the hot weather season (mid-March to mid-June) in Karnataka are called
33.x: Karnataka's hot-weather thunderstorm rains are mango showers (coffee areas also call them blossom showers). Kalbaisakhi belongs to West Bengal and Loo is a hot dry wind.

33.s:
Assertion (A) Convectional rains occur during pre-monsoon summer in India.
Reason (R) Such rains occur due to adiabatic cooling.
Codes
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
33.x: Pre-monsoon rains are convectional: intense heating makes the air rise, cool adiabatically, condense and give thunderstorms – so both A and R are true and R explains A.

33.s: In India dust storms commonly occur in the month of
33.x: Dust storms (andhis) are commonest in May, the hottest pre-monsoon month, over Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and western UP.

33.s: From the following states, which one usually witnesses the blossom shower?
33.x: Blossom showers are pre-monsoon showers of Kerala (and Karnataka) that make coffee flowers blossom.

33.s: Under which ministry was the 'National Monsoon Mission' launched?
33.src: APPSC Asst. Chemist, Asst. Director, Civil Asst. Surgeons, T
33.x: The National Monsoon Mission was launched in 2012 by the Ministry of Earth Sciences, through IITM Pune and the IMD.

33.s:
Match the following climatic phenomena with their respective characteristics related to India.
A. Southwest Monsoon
B. Northeast Monsoon
C. Western Disturbances
D. El Nino Effect 1. Causes drought-like conditions in parts of India during certain years 2. Brings winter and post-monsoon rainfall 3. Main source of rainfall for the Indian subcontinent during June - September 4. Responsible for heavy rainfall in Tamil Nadu during October-December
33.src: APPSC Forest Range Officer Screening Test General Studies &
33.x: SW monsoon – main June–September rain (3); NE monsoon – Tamil Nadu's October–December rain (4); western disturbances – winter rain (2); El Nino – drought-like conditions (1).

Match Koeppen's climatic types with region of occurrence:
List I
A. Aw
B. Dfc
C. Cwg
D. Amw
E. As List II
I. Coromandel coast
II. Western coastal region of India, south of Mumbai

33.x: Aw (tropical savanna) – peninsular plateau; Dfc – Sikkim, Arunachal and parts of Assam; Cwg – Ganga plain, E Rajasthan, Malwa; Amw – west coast south of Mumbai; As – Coromandel coast.

33.s: Which of the following States coast is known as Coromandel coast?
33.src: APPSC Group-I Services Preliminary (Screening) Test (Notification of 2008) - General Studies & Mental Ability, re-examination held 25-10-2010 · Q6
33.x: The Coromandel Coast is the eastern coast of Tamil Nadu (and southern Andhra).

33.s: In India dust storms commonly occur in the month of
33.src: APPSC Group-I Services Preliminary (Screening) Test (Notification Nos. 15/2011 & 18/2011) - General Studies & Mental Ability, Booklet Series A, held 27-05-2012 · Q122
33.x: Dust storms are most common in north-west India in May (hot season).

33.s: India's hot weather season, brought by the Sun's northward march, lasts which months?
xs: The Sun's northward march brings the **hot weather season (March-May)**.
33.x: The Sun's northward march brings the hot weather season (March-May).

33.s: Which Koeppen code applies to the Ganga plain?
xs: **Cwg** — Ganga plain (monsoon with dry winter); **BShw** — north-west India.
33.x: Cwg — Ganga plain (monsoon with dry winter); BShw — north-west India.

33.s: Which hills, funnel-shaped, give the world's highest rainfall at Mawsynram?
xs: **Western Ghats** = heavy **orographic** rain on the **windward** west coast; **Meghalaya Hills** = **Mawsynram**, world's highest rainfall.
33.x: Western Ghats = heavy orographic rain on the windward west coast; Meghalaya Hills = Mawsynram, world's highest rainfall.

33.s: Which range gives heavy orographic rainfall on India's windward west coast?
xs: **Western Ghats** = heavy **orographic** rain on the **windward** west coast; **Meghalaya Hills** = **Mawsynram**, world's highest rainfall.
xa: **Interior Deccan** has low rainfall in the **Western Ghats rain shadow**.
Western Ghats wettest spots: **Agumbe**, **Hulikal**.
33.x: Western Ghats = heavy orographic rain on the windward west coast; Meghalaya Hills = Mawsynram, world's highest rainfall.

33.s: The southward shift of the doldrums brings heavy rain to southern states, giving what rainfall pattern?
xs: The **southward shift of the doldrums** brings **heavy rain in southern states** (**bimodal rainfall**).
33.x: The southward shift of the doldrums brings heavy rain in southern states (bimodal rainfall).

33.s: In which direction do winter monsoon winds blow?
o: From the equator to the poles
xs: **Summer:** From **sea to land**; **winter:** from **land to sea**
33.x: Summer: From sea to land; winter: from land to sea

33.s: Under the westerlies, temperate cyclones generally move in which direction?
xs: B is false: under the **westerlies** they move **from west to east**.
xa: Tropical cyclones move **east to west** with the **trade winds**.
33.x: B is false: under the westerlies they move from west to east.

33.s: In which season do Western Disturbances mainly affect north-western India?
xs: They reach NW India in winter at the **occluded stage**.
xa: They occur mainly in **winter**, not summer.
They bring **winter rainfall** and **snowfall** to mountains — important for **Rabi crops**.
33.x: They reach NW India in winter at the occluded stage.

33.s: Cherry or coffee blossoms showers aid coffee flowering in which state?
xs: **Cherry / coffee blossoms**: Karnataka; Coffee flowering [GK]
33.x: Cherry / coffee blossoms: Karnataka; Coffee flowering [GK]

33.s: How does the rainfall from Western Disturbances change across the north-western plain?
xs: Their **rainfall decreases from west to east** across the **northwestern plain**.
33.x: Their rainfall decreases from west to east across the northwestern plain.

33.s: The distribution of monsoon rainfall in India is controlled mainly by?
xs: Distribution is controlled mainly by **relief**.
33.x: Distribution is controlled mainly by relief.

33.s: Who proposed the classical thermal theory of the monsoon (1686)?
xs: This is the classical **thermal** theory of Sir Edmund **Halley** (**1686**); the pattern reverses in winter.
33.x: This is the classical thermal theory of Sir Edmund Halley (1686); the pattern reverses in winter.

o: Northward shift over the Ganga plain
Southward shift over the Indian Ocean

33.s: As the ITCZ shifts north, the south-east trades cross the equator and become?

The heating of the Tibetan Plateau contributes to the southwest monsoon by:
o: Creating an upper-air anticyclone and strengthening the tropical easterly jet
Blocking all cross-equatorial winds in the Arabian Sea
Creating a permanent surface high and weakening the tropical easterly jet
Producing the subtropical westerly jet south of the Himalayas in summer
33.x: The Tibetan Plateau, at about 5,000 m, acts as a heat island in summer. Its intense heating produces an upper-air anticyclone and strengthens the tropical easterly jet.
xs: Tibetan heating creates an **upper-air anticyclone** and a **stronger Tropical Easterly Jet** — option **(1)**.

93.s: Kanha National Park belongs to which one among the following biogeographical areas in the world?
93.x:
Keys differ: most (CDS 2011 key, ICAR set) give Tropical Dry Forests; some guides (Byju's, examrobot) give Tropical Sub-humid Forests (web search, Nov 2026).
Kanha's sal and dry deciduous forests place it in the Tropical Dry Forest biogeographic zone (the CDS key).

93.s: Two important rivers - one with its source in Jharkhand (and known by a different name in Odisha), and another, with its source in Odishamerge at a place only a short distance from the coast of Bay of Bengal before flowing into the sea. 93.x: The Brahmani (formed by the South Koel from Jharkhand and the Sankh) and the Baitarani (from Odisha) meet near the coast at Bhitarkanika, a mangrove protected area. Simlipal is inland; Chandipur and Gopalpur are beaches.

93.s: Which of the following National Parks is unique in being a swamp with floating vegetation that supports a rich biodiversity?
93.x: Keibul Lamjao (Manipur), on Loktak Lake, is the only floating national park – a swamp of floating phumdis with rich biodiversity (Sangai deer).

93.x: Keibul Lamjao (Manipur), on Loktak Lake, is the only floating national park – a swamp of floating phumdis.

93.x: Keibul Lamjao National Park floats on Loktak Lake, Manipur. Dal and Wular are in Kashmir and Kolleru in Andhra Pradesh.

39.x: Laterite is porous and well drained with poor water-holding capacity, so 'moisture retentive with a large clay factor' (a black-soil trait) is not true. It is deficient in lime and nitrogen, leached, and a good building material.

39.x: Gypsum supplies calcium that displaces sodium, so with leaching water it is the long-term remedy for saline-alkaline soil. Rock phosphate, manure, urea, dry farming and contour cultivation do not remove salts.

o: Use of Gypsum in the fields

lime decreases the acidity of soil.
lime decreases the basicity of soil.

o: Soil getting very deficient in plant nutrients.
Soil getting enriched with plant nutrients.
39.x: Soil impoverishment means the soil has become very deficient in plant nutrients. Erosion is a cause, and enrichment is the opposite.

39.s: Salinisation occurs when the irrigation water accumulated in the soil evaporates, leaving behind salts and minerals. What are the effects of salinisation on the irrigated land?
o: It greatly increases the crop production.
It fills the air spaces in the soil with water.
39.x: Salts left behind by evaporating irrigation water clog soil pores and make some soils impermeable. Salinisation lowers yields; waterlogging, not salinisation, raises the water table.

39.x: Gujarat has the largest area of saline soil (Rann of Kutch, Gulf of Khambhat). Uttar Pradesh leads in alkali soil.

39.x: Zinc is the micronutrient most widely deficient in Indian soils, ahead of iron, manganese and copper.

Match the following Geographical Feature with Historical / Cultural Impact: 1. Eastern Ghats
2. Krishna-Godavari Deltas
3. Bay of Bengal Coastline
4. Rayalaseema Region
5. Visakhapatnam Port A. Sustained agricultural wealth and dynasties
B. Fostered maritime trade with Southeast Asia

31.s:
Statement: The geography of Andhra Pradesh has shaped its economic landscape in multiple ways:
1. The Eastern Ghats restricted inland trade routes.
2. The Krishna-Godavari deltas supported rice cultivation.
3. The Bay of Bengal coastline enabled maritime commerce.
4. The Rayalaseema region faced water scarcity challenges.
5. Visakhapatnam's port boosted colonial trade.
Question: Which of these factors most significantly contributed to Andhra Pradesh's historical economic prosperity?
31.src: APPSC Assistant Tribal Welfare Officer in A.P. Tribal Welfar
31.x: Agrarian wealth from the Krishna-Godavari deltas (2), maritime commerce along the Bay of Bengal (3) and Visakhapatnam's port trade (5) drove prosperity. The Ghats' barrier (1) and Rayalaseema's water scarcity (4) were constraints.

40.s: Weathering of granite and gneiss is associated with the formation of which soil in Andhra Pradesh?
40.x: In Andhra Pradesh, weathering of granite and gneiss gives rise to red soils. Weathering of basalt is associated with black soils.
xs: Weathering of **granite and gneiss** gives **red soil** in AP — option **(2)** is correct.
**Black soils** come from weathering of **basalt**.
xa: Physical weathering = **no chemical change** (exfoliation, frost wedging).
Chemical weathering: **solution, carbonation, oxidation, hydration, hydrolysis**.
AP deltas: Godavari-Krishna delta plains = "**rice granary of South India**".
40.tq: Match the parent rock with the resulting soil type.

40.s: Deltaic alluvial soils cover about what share of Andhra Pradesh?
Black (regur) soil covers about what share of Andhra Pradesh?
Which is the smallest of the principal soils of AP, at about 1 per cent?
xs: **laterite** is the **smallest**, about **1%** of the State.
xa: ⚠ Order by area: **Red > Black > Deltaic alluvium > Laterite**.
40.x: laterite is the smallest, about 1% of the State.

40.s: Which soil type dominates the Konaseema and Krishna-Godavari delta areas?
xs: **Konaseema** and the **Krishna-Godavari deltas** are **deltaic alluvium** areas, not red soil.
40.x: Konaseema and the Krishna-Godavari deltas are deltaic alluvium areas, not red soil.

40.s: Black soils occupy about what fraction of Andhra Pradesh's land area?
xs: Black soil covers ~**25%** — about one-fourth.
40.x: Black soil covers ~25% — about one-fourth.

40.s: Deep black soils in AP occur at Adoni and which other place?
xs: **deep black** soil occurs at **Adoni and Alur**.
40.x: deep black soil occurs at Adoni and Alur.

40.s: Which river basin in AP contains black soils along with Guntur and Prakasam?
xs: Black soil occurs in the **Kunderu basin** and **Guntur, Palnadu, Prakasam, Kurnool**.
40.x: Black soil occurs in the Kunderu basin and Guntur, Palnadu, Prakasam, Kurnool.

40.s: Deltaic alluvium in AP is laid down by the Godavari and which river?
xs: It is laid down as **river-borne silt** by the **Godavari and Krishna**, **renewed with silt each flood**.
xa: Found in the **Godavari and Krishna deltas**, **Konaseema**, Nellore, Guntur.
40.x: It is laid down as river-borne silt by the Godavari and Krishna, renewed with silt each flood.

40.s: Which soil is most suitable for the fertile agricultural tracts of the Krishna-Godavari deltas?
40.x: The Krishna-Godavari deltaic tracts are characterised by highly fertile deltaic alluvial soil.
xs: The fertile **Krishna-Godavari deltas** have **deltaic alluvial soil** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Shallow red soil** marks **Rayalaseema**; **laterite** is acidic and of poor fertility; **skeletal** soils have no nutritive value.
xa: Alluvium is renewed with **silt each flood**.
It is rich in **potash and lime**.
Alluvium → **rice** (paddy) and **sugarcane**.
40.tq: Use the regional soil-crop setting to identify the most suitable soil.

40.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of areas associated with laterite soils in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai, Kadapa and Nandyal only
Kurnool, Nandyal, Palnadu, Bapatla and Guntur
Ellavaram, Peddapuram, Kavali, Kovvur, Gudur and Sullurpeta
Konaseema, Krishna delta, Godavari delta and Nellore delta
40.x: Ellavaram, Peddapuram, Kavali, Kovvur, Gudur and Sullurpeta are listed as laterite-soil areas. Laterite also occurs in elevated areas such as Satyavedu and Puttur and in coastal pockets.
xs: **Ellavaram, Peddapuram, Kavali, Kovvur, Gudur and Sullurpeta** are coastal **laterite** areas — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai, Kadapa, Nandyal** are **red** soil; **Kurnool, Palnadu, Bapatla, Guntur** **black**; **Konaseema** and the deltas **alluvium**.
xa: Elevated laterite: **Satyavedu, Puttur**.
Inland laterite belt: **Tirupati, Gudur, Sullurpet, Satyavedu, Puttur**.
Pockets: Nellore, Srikakulam, East Godavari, Anakapalli, Visakhapatnam.
40.tq: Check whether every location in the option belongs to the same soil-distribution group.

40.s: Heavily eroded tracts of Rayalaseema may develop skeletal soils that are characterised by:
o: High nutrient value and deep profiles
High water retention and abundant humus
40.x: Severe erosion in Rayalaseema can leave skeletal soils with no nutritive value.
xs: Skeletal soils in heavily eroded tracts have **no nutritive value** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Fresh silt** deposition renews **deltaic alluvium**, the opposite case.
xa: Rayalaseema red soils are **shallow** with low organic matter.
**Podu** (shifting) cultivation strips topsoil in **ASR, Parvathipuram Manyam**.
Responses: **watershed** development + **MGNREGA** soil-and-water works.
40.tq: Infer the soil-quality outcome from the stated erosion process.

40.s: Heavy chemical use degrades soils in the Krishna paddy belt and which crop belt of Guntur?
xs: **heavy chemical use** in the **Guntur chilli + Krishna paddy** belts.
40.x: heavy chemical use in the Guntur chilli + Krishna paddy belts.

40.s: The nine rainfed districts are the eight Rayalaseema districts and which other?
xs: The **9** rainfed districts = **8 Rayalaseema districts + Prakasam**, not Nellore.
40.x: The 9 rainfed districts = 8 Rayalaseema districts + Prakasam, not Nellore.

40.s: On which soil does black gram do best?
xs: **Red, green and horse gram** suit **red soil**, while **black gram** does best on **black soil**
xa: Black gram on black soils is a **UPSC** fact.
Black soil main crops: **cotton, chillies, tobacco, turmeric**.
40.x: Red, green and horse gram suit red soil, while black gram does best on black soil

40.s: Red gram, green gram and horse gram are suited to which soil?
xs: **Red, green and horse gram** suit **red soil**, while **black gram** does best on **black soil**
xa: Red soil also carries **groundnut**, castor, millets.
40.x: Red, green and horse gram suit red soil, while black gram does best on black soil

40.s: Millets, pulses and groundnut are typically grown on which soil?
xs: **Red** soil grows **millets**, **pulses**, **groundnut**.
xa: AP red soil pulses: **red gram, green gram, horse gram**; also castor.
40.x: Red soil grows millets, pulses, groundnut.

40.s: Coffee, rubber and cashew are typically grown on which soil?
xs: **Laterite** soil grows **tea**, **coffee**, **rubber**, **cashew**.
40.x: Laterite soil grows tea, coffee, rubber, cashew.

40.s: Which characteristic of black soil is specifically associated with drying?
o: It becomes permanently waterlogged on drying
It loses all mineral constituents on drying
40.x: Black soil swells when wet and develops deep cracks on drying, which lets it self-plough.
xs: Black soil **develops cracks on drying** — option **(3)**.
The deep cracks let it **turn itself over** — **"self-ploughing"**.
This goes with its **clayey** texture and **very high water retention**.
xa: Black soil is particularly suitable for **cotton**.
AP black soils are **neutral to strongly alkaline**.
⚠ Desert soil, by contrast, is **sandy** with **low moisture retention**.
40.tq: Recall the features of black soil.

40.s: Which kind of soil is found in the arid Thar Desert?
xs: The **Thar Desert** has **desert / arid** soil — sandy, low organic matter.
xa: The incorrect statement is "**Laterite soil develops mainly in the arid Thar Desert**"
40.x: The Thar Desert has desert / arid soil — sandy, low organic matter.

40.s: Laterite soil develops in AP, Karnataka and which part of Maharashtra?
xs: It develops in **Andhra Pradesh**, **South Maharashtra**, **Karnataka**, among others.
40.x: It develops in Andhra Pradesh, South Maharashtra, Karnataka, among others.

40.s: Fertile alluvial soil of AP's Krishna-Godavari deltas supports rice and which other crop?
xs: That fertility is why it grows **rice** (all four delta areas) and **sugarcane**.
40.x: That fertility is why it grows rice (all four delta areas) and sugarcane.

40.s: Which crop is matched with laterite soil in AP?
xs: **Red** → **groundnut** (c-iv); **Laterite** → **cashew** (d-ii).
40.x: Red → groundnut (c-iv); Laterite → cashew (d-ii).

40.s: Which crop is matched with red soil in AP?
xs: **Red** → **groundnut** (c-iv); **Laterite** → **cashew** (d-ii).
40.x: Red → groundnut (c-iv); Laterite → cashew (d-ii).

40.s: Which crop is matched with alluvial soil in AP?
xs: **Alluvial** → **rice** (a-iii); **Black** → **cotton** (b-i).
40.x: Alluvial → rice (a-iii); Black → cotton (b-i).

40.s: Unclassified black soils of AP are found in West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur and which place?
xs: **Unclassified black** → **West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Mid-Kurnool, NW Cuddapah, Thadipatri** (c-iv); **Red** → **Rayalaseema** (d-i).
40.x: Unclassified black → West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Mid-Kurnool, NW Cuddapah, Thadipatri (c-iv); Red → Rayalaseema (d-i).

40.s: Which region of AP is typed by red soil?
xs: **Unclassified black** → **West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Mid-Kurnool, NW Cuddapah, Thadipatri** (c-iv); **Red** → **Rayalaseema** (d-i).
40.x: Unclassified black → West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Mid-Kurnool, NW Cuddapah, Thadipatri (c-iv); Red → Rayalaseema (d-i).

40.s: Which bedrock underlies much of Andhra Pradesh?
xs: **Granitoid-gneiss** bedrock underlies much of AP
40.x: Granitoid-gneiss bedrock underlies much of AP

40.s: The red colour of red soils is mainly due to?
xs: The red colour comes from **ferric oxides**.
40.x: The red colour comes from ferric oxides.

Towards which directions do Deccan black soils become thinner?
xs: **Very deep black soils** occur in the **north-western Deccan Plateau** and thin out towards the **east and south**
40.x: Very deep black soils occur in the north-western Deccan Plateau and thin out towards the east and south

40.s: Black soils of AP are mainly derived from crystalline schists, basic gneiss and which rock?
xs: Black soils derive from **Deccan Trap basalt** (Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur, East Godavari) + **crystalline schists** and **basic gneiss**.
40.x: Black soils derive from Deccan Trap basalt (Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur, East Godavari) + crystalline schists and basic gneiss.

40.s: Black soils of AP are rich in calcium, magnesium and which nutrient?
xs: They are **rich in calcium, potash, magnesium** (Ca, K, Mg).
xa: ⚠ Rich in **Ca, K, Mg** = black; **potash and lime** = alluvium; **iron and aluminium oxides** = laterite.
40.x: They are rich in calcium, potash, magnesium (Ca, K, Mg).

40.s: What is the water-retention capacity of black soils?
xs: **high water retention**; deep cracks when dry → **"self-ploughing"**.
40.x: high water retention; deep cracks when dry → "self-ploughing".

40.s: Deltaic alluvial soils of AP are rich in potash and which other nutrient?
xs: It is **rich in potash and lime**.
40.x: It is rich in potash and lime.

40.s: What is the moisture retention of AP's porous, loamy deltaic alluvium?
xs: Deltaic alluvium is **porous and loamy** with **high moisture retention**.
40.x: Deltaic alluvium is porous and loamy with high moisture retention.

40.s: Which substances are leached out during the formation of laterite soils?
xs: Laterites form under **high temperature and heavy rainfall** through **intense leaching** of **silica and lime**.
40.x: Laterites form under high temperature and heavy rainfall through intense leaching of silica and lime.

40.s: Laterite soils are rich in hydrated oxides of iron and which other metal?
xs: It is rich in hydrated **iron and aluminium oxides**.
40.x: It is rich in hydrated iron and aluminium oxides.

40.s: What is the usual colour of laterite soils?
What is the general fertility of laterite soils?

40.x: Laterite has poor fertility; the standard fact is poor in nitrogen.

40.s: What effect does alkalinity (high pH) have on plant nutrient availability?
Which soil type is associated with acidic conditions, while black soil generally shows a neutral to strongly alkaline tendency?
40.x: Laterite soils are associated with acidic conditions, whereas black soils are generally neutral to strongly alkaline.
xs: **Laterite** soils are **acidic**, while black soils are neutral to strongly alkaline — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Deltaic alluvium** is rich in **potash and lime**, not acidic.
xa: Laterite acidity follows intense **leaching** of **silica and lime**.
Alkalinity cuts **nutrient availability**.
Black soils are **fine, clayey**, from **Deccan Trap basalt**.
40.tq: Discriminate between the acidic and alkaline soil associations.

40.s: Saline soils of the Rayalaseema plateau contain high amounts of salt and what else?
xs: **Rayalaseema plateau:** Saline soils high in lime and salt → unfit for cropping
40.x: Rayalaseema plateau: Saline soils high in lime and salt → unfit for cropping

40.s: Salinity in AP's delta regions is caused by poor drainage and which other factor?
xs: Delta salinity comes from **poor drainage + faulty irrigation**, plus **saline water intrusion**.
40.x: Delta salinity comes from poor drainage + faulty irrigation, plus saline water intrusion.

40.s: Which of the following best describes the characteristic condition of Rayalaseema's red soils?
o: Permanently waterlogged and rich in humus
Shallow, with low moisture retention and low organic matter
Deep, highly moist and rich in organic matter
40.x: Rayalaseema's red soils are shallow and have low moisture-retention capacity and low organic matter.
xs: Rayalaseema's red soils are **shallow, with low moisture retention and low organic matter** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Clayey, alkaline, self-ploughing** describes **black** soil.
xa: Red soils are **poor in N, P, organic matter**.
**Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai** face **desertification** and **wind erosion**.
Eroded tracts develop **skeletal soils** with no nutritive value.

40.s: What effect does fresh flood silt have on the deltaic alluvium?
xs: Fresh flood silt **renews** deltaic alluvium; it is not a degradation cause.
40.x: Fresh flood silt renews deltaic alluvium; it is not a degradation cause.

40.s: APCNF natural farming aims to restore which soil property?

40.s: Alluvial soil is generally rich in potash, lime and which other nutrient?

40.x: I is correct: alluvium is generally rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime.

40.s: Alluvial soil is generally poor in nitrogen and what else?

40.s: Which soil is generally of low fertility due to leaching?

40.x: Black soil is black because of its mineral composition — iron- and titanium-related constituents.

97.s: Thomas Malthus, in his theory of population, postulated that population increases in a:
o: Geometrical progression, while food supply increases arithmetically
Arithmetical progression, while food supply increases geometrically
Constant proportion, while food supply remains unchanged
Linear progression, while food supply increases geometrically
97.x: Malthus argued that population tends to grow geometrically or exponentially, whereas food and resources increase only arithmetically.
xs: **Malthus**: population grows in a **geometrical** (exponential) progression while **food grows arithmetically** — option **(1)**.
Unchecked growth thus leads to **scarcity and famine**; option 2 reverses the two.
xa: His work: **An Essay on the Principle of Population** (**1798**).
Checks: **preventive** (lower births) and **positive** (raise deaths).
Neo-Malthusian **Paul R. Ehrlich** wrote **The Population Bomb** (**1968**).
97.tq: Test the paired comparison carefully; APPSC commonly reverses the two rates.

97.s: Which one of the following is a preventive check in Malthusian population theory?
97.x: Preventive checks reduce the birth rate and include moral restraint, late marriage and celibacy. Famine, disease and war are positive checks because they increase mortality.
xs: **Late marriage** is a **preventive check** — option **(3)**.
Preventive checks **lower births**: moral restraint, late marriage, celibacy.
**Famine, disease and war** are **positive checks** — they **raise deaths**.
xa: ⚠ **Preventive** = fewer births; **Positive** = more deaths.
Malthus: population **geometric**, food **arithmetic**.
Essay published **1798**.
97.tq: Separate measures affecting births from events increasing deaths.

97.s: Which one of the following is a major criticism of the Malthusian prediction?
o: Population has declined continuously because of famine
Technology, innovation and sustainable resource management have exceeded his predictions
Industrialisation eliminated all regional differences in population distribution
Food production has remained completely static since the eighteenth century
97.x: Technological progress, innovation and sustainable resource management have enabled resources and food production to grow faster than Malthus anticipated.
xs: Critics note that **technology, innovation and sustainable resource management** have **outpaced Malthus's predictions** — option **(2)**.
Food output has not stayed static, and population has not declined through famine.
xa: **India**: fertility fell to **replacement** without famine (**2026**).
"Population Bomb" fears are now overtaken by **fertility decline**.
Malthus's **positive checks**: famine, disease, war.
97.tq: Choose the precise criticism rather than an absolute statement about population trends.

97.s: According to Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), population and food supply tend to grow respectively in:
97.x: Malthus held that population grows in geometric progression (1, 2, 4, 8...) while food supply grows only in arithmetic progression (1, 2, 3, 4...), so population outruns food. Option A reverses the two; C and D wrongly give both the same progression.
xs: Population grows in **geometric** and food in **arithmetic progression** — option **(2)** is correct.

xa: UPPSC 2024 asked these Malthusian blanks (**geometric, arithmetic**).
**Positive checks** (famine, disease, war) raise the death rate; **preventive checks** (moral restraint, late marriage) lower the birth rate.

98.s: A country with a crude birth rate of 44 and a crude death rate of 11 would have an annual rate of natural increase of-
98.x: Natural increase = CBR − CDR = 44 − 11 = 33 per 1,000, which is 3.3% a year. 33% and 0.33% misplace the decimal.

98.s:
Natural Growth of population is the outcome of which of the following? I. Crude Birth Rate
II. Crude Death Rate III. Migration
IV. Marriage
Select the correct answer from the codes given below.
98.x: Natural growth = births − deaths, so it comes from the crude birth rate and crude death rate (I and II). Migration is a separate component of actual growth, and marriage is not a component.

98.s: The term ‘demographic gap’ signifies the difference
o: between the birth and the death rate.
98.x: The demographic gap is the difference between the birth rate and the death rate. It widens in the second stage of the demographic transition, when deaths fall first. It has nothing to do with sex ratio, age or the child–woman ratio.

98.s: Consider the following statement and answer the question. Statement: It took more than a million years for the world human population to attain the one billion mark. But it took only 12 years for it to rise from 5 billion to 6 billion. Which of the following time period can be represented from the statement?
98.x: World population reached 5 billion in 1987 and 6 billion in 1999, only 12 years later, which shows the late-20th-century population explosion. 1974 was the 4-billion mark and 2011 the 7-billion mark.

98.s: The dependency ratio is calculated as the ratio of which of the following?
o: Population aged 15–64 years to the population aged 65 years and above
Population aged 0–14 years and 65 years and above to the working-age population
Working-age population to the total population aged 0–14 years
Total non-working population to the total population below 14 years
98.x: The dependency ratio compares dependants—those aged 0–14 years and 65 years or above—with the working-age population.
xs: Dependency ratio = dependants aged **0-14 and 65+** / **working-age population** — option **(2)**.
The other options leave out a dependant group or invert the ratio.
xa: A **lower** ratio → potential **demographic dividend**.
Economic Survey warning (2025-26): the dependency ratio will **double**.
Highest working-age share: **UAE 85.7%**, **Qatar 85.6%**.
98.tq: Use the exact age groups and denominator to distinguish the demographic indicator.

98.s: According to the Economic Survey 2025–26, which one of the following is identified as a likely consequence of the dependency ratio doubling?
o: The disappearance of the working-age population
A complete decline in demand for healthcare services
Geriatric care becoming a growth job sector
A permanent fall in the elderly population
98.x: The Economic Survey 2025–26 cautions that a doubling of the dependency ratio will increase the importance of geriatric care as a growth-oriented employment sector.
xs: A **doubling dependency ratio** makes **geriatric care a growth job sector** — option **(3)**.
The elderly population is rising, not falling: **130.5 mn → 325.3 mn** by **2051**.
xa: Median age: **28 → 40**.
Tamil Nadu old-age dependency: **20.6 → 32.7** (2021-2036).
98.tq: Link the projected demographic trend with its sectoral employment implication.

98.s: Which of the following best expresses the significance of the demographic dividend window for India?
o: It has already closed because the dependency ratio is rising in every State.
It closes after 2041, making skilling and employment generation time-bound priorities.
It closes in 2031, after which only fertility reduction is required.
It will remain open indefinitely because the working-age population always increases.
98.x: The demographic dividend window is expected to close after 2041; therefore, skilling and creation of suitable jobs are time-bound priorities.
xs: India's **dividend window closes after 2041**, so **skilling and jobs** are time-bound priorities — option **(2)**.
It has not already closed, and it will not stay open indefinitely.
xa: A **lower** dependency ratio creates the potential dividend.
The dependency ratio will **double** → geriatric care a growth job sector.
98.tq: Identify the precise deadline and connect it with the stated policy priorities.

98.s: A region has a crude birth rate of 44 and a crude death rate of 11 per thousand. Its rate of natural increase is:

Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct
51.x:
Most books follow NCERT ('western temperate cyclones') and key (a); printed key here: (A) false, (R) true. Strictly: western disturbances are temperate (extra-tropical) cyclones, so R as worded ('tropical') is false, which would give (b) (NextGen Indian Geography 07 p.4).

51.s:
Statement: Sequential cropping involves planting multiple crops in a sequence on the same field within a year, without intercrop competition. Intercropping leads to crop intensification in both time and space dimensions, with competition between crops during their growth stages. Sole cropping is the practice of growing a single crop variety on a field, not multiple varieties simultaneously. The Land Equivalent Ratio (LER) is used to measure the productivity advantage of intercropping compared to sole cropping.
Conclusion: The correct practice for measuring the productivity of intercropping in comparison to sole cropping is the use of the Land Equivalent Ratio (LER).
Which of the following can be drawn from the above statement?
A) Sequential cropping and intercropping both involve growing multiple crops on the same field simultaneously.
B) Sole cropping refers to growing a single crop variety, not multiple varieties.
C) The Land Equivalent Ratio (LER) measures the productivity of sequential cropping.
D) Intercropping has no impact on the productivity of the land.
51.src: APPSC Junior Assistant in Dr. NTR University of Health Scien
51.x: Only B follows: sole cropping is a single variety; sequential cropping is not simultaneous, LER measures intercropping (not sequential cropping), and intercropping does affect productivity.

Statement: The processes for formulating cropping patterns in agro-ecological cells involve fitting crop growth cycles to the prevailing lengths of growing periods, incorporating turn-around times between crops, and determining acceptable intercropping levels for various inputs and crop types.
Conclusion: Therefore, these processes enable cropping patterns to be effectively adapted to local climatic conditions and crop types, ensuring optimal agricultural yields.
Which of the following best supports the conclusion drawn from the statement above?
1. Cropping patterns are designed to accommodate the unique growth requirements of different crops within specific agro-ecological contexts.
2. Fixed turn-around periods may restrict the flexibility of cropping systems to adapt to varying agricultural practices.
3. Intercropping practices are uniformly applied across all crop types to maximise resource efficiency in diverse conditions.
4. The model does not consider the growth requirements of perennial crops, which can limit sustainable agricultural development.
51.src: APPSC Junior Assistant in Dr. NTR University of Health Scien
51.x: Only 1 supports the conclusion: patterns are fitted to crop growth needs in each agro-ecological cell; 2-4 weaken or contradict it.
